:::{#def-gram-matrix}
#### Gram matrix

The **Gram matrix** of an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$
is the $n \times n$ matrix $\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-gram-matrix}
#### A Gram matrix and its entries

Let $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$,
with columns $\vecf{a}_1 = (1, 1, 0)$ and $\vecf{a}_2 = (0, 1, 1)$. Then

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-transpose)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0 & 1 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 1 \\
0 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 0 & 0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(@def-matrix-mult)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.
&& \text{(multiply and add)}
\ea
$$

Row $i$ of $\tp{\matr{A}}$ is column $i$ of $\matr{A}$,
so entry $(i, j)$ of the Gram matrix is the dot product $\vecf{a}_i \cdot \vecf{a}_j$:
for instance,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vecf{a}_1 \cdot \vecf{a}_2 &= 0 + 1 + 0 \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

is entry $(1, 2)$.

:::
